title: Stratford-upon-Avon
subtitle: Shakespeare the businessman
intro: Sunday afternoon in Stratford-upon-Avon. First, film the places that close early. Then walk Shakespeare's life in order: the house he was born in, his school, the house he got rich enough to buy, and his grave.

acts.label: Act 1 · 1564: born into trouble
acts.narrative: His father made gloves, rose to the top job in the town, then lost his money. The first record of the family is a fine for a pile of rubbish in this street.

acts.label: Act 2 · School, marriage, London
acts.tagline: Free school, married at 18, then gone.
acts.narrative: A free school paid for by the town. Then marriage at 18, three children by 20, and off to London.

acts.label: Act 3 · The businessman
acts.tagline: Rich from owning, not from writing.
acts.narrative: He comes back into view in London. He gets rich owning a share of a theatre company, buys one of the biggest houses in town, gets the family a coat of arms, and loses his only son.

acts.label: Act 4 · The grave, and what he left
acts.tagline: A grave he paid for. Words we still use.
acts.narrative: He bought the right to be buried by the altar. His friends saved his plays. And his words are still in the way we talk.

see: Harvard House on High Street (1596). It was the family home of John Harvard's mother. Harvard University is named after him.

new-place.name: Shakespeare's New Place
new-place.story: You filmed the garden at 2:10. Now tell the story from the gate on Chapel Street.
new-place.onCamera: For about seven years after he left, nobody knows where Shakespeare was. Historians call them the lost years. When he appears again, he's in London, working as an actor and a writer. Then, at 33, he buys a house on this spot, one of the biggest in his home town. So how does a glove-maker's son get that rich? Not by writing.
facts: He didn't get rich from writing. He got rich because he owned a share of his acting company, and a share of the Globe Theatre in London.

In 1596 he finally got his father that coat of arms, an official family badge that only gentlemen could have, passed from father to son. The motto was 'Not without right.' That same year, his only son, Hamnet, died. He was 11.
new-place.closeOnCamera: So where's the house? In the 1750s a priest called Francis Gastrell owned it. Tourists kept coming, so he cut down Shakespeare's mulberry tree. Then, after an argument with the town about tax, he knocked the whole house down in 1759. The town was so angry that he had to leave. Shakespeare spent his last years here, and died here in 1616. He's buried just down the road.

church-street.name: The Guild Chapel and his school
church-street.story: Outside only: the chapel closes at 4 and the schoolroom's last entry is 4:15. The schoolroom is upstairs in the old Guildhall, the medieval town hall.
church-street.onCamera: This is almost certainly where Shakespeare went to school. Think about that. The boy who went on to write Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet and Macbeth sat his lessons here, in a room upstairs. And what he learned here, and what he didn't, is still argued about today.
facts: It was a free school for boys from the town. Lessons were in Latin, from early morning to late afternoon, Monday to Saturday.
Nobody can prove he came here. But it was free, it was five minutes from his house, and his father had been the head of the town.
church-street.closeOnCamera: He never went to university. That's why some people still say a nobleman must have written his plays. Almost every historian disagrees. And then his life moves fast. At 18 he married Anne Hathaway. She was 26, and already pregnant. By 20 he had three children. Then he left them here in Stratford, and went to London.

holy-trinity.name: Holy Trinity Church
holy-trinity.story: You filmed the grave at 2:33. The church is closed now, so tell this part outside, on the avenue of lime trees. If the gate is shut, use the riverbank, where you can see the spire.
holy-trinity.onCamera: This is where Shakespeare is buried. He died in 1616, aged 52. In his will, the only thing he left his wife by name was his 'second-best bed'. People still argue about what he meant by it. And how he got this grave tells you a lot about the man. He paid for it.
facts: Most people were buried outside, in the churchyard. In 1605 he paid £440, a fortune at the time, for a share of the church's income. That gave him the right to be buried in here, next to the altar.

Seven years after he died, two actors from his company printed his plays in one big book, the First Folio. Eighteen of the plays had never been printed before, including Macbeth and The Tempest. Without that book, we would probably have lost them.
holy-trinity.closeOnCamera: Now, his gravestone. It says: 'Cursed be he that moves my bones.' In 2016, scientists scanned the grave with radar. The head end looks disturbed. That fits an old story that someone stole his skull. The church isn't convinced. So that's his life, from that house on Henley Street to here. But the story doesn't end with his death.

birthplace.name: Shakespeare's Birthplace
birthplace.angle: 1564 · Born into a family in trouble
birthplace.story: Timed entry: use your slot. Last entry is 4:30. This is where the walk through his life begins.
birthplace.onCamera: This is where it all starts. William Shakespeare was born in this house in 1564. Today he's probably the most famous writer in the world. But he didn't start out important. When he was a boy, his family was in trouble. And I think that explains everything he did later.
facts: The first record of his family is right here. In April 1552, his father was fined 12 pence for leaving a pile of rubbish and dung in this street.

His father made gloves. He rose to the top job in the town, like a mayor. Then his business failed, he got into debt, and his request for a family coat of arms went nowhere. William grew up watching his family lose its money and its position.
birthplace.closeOnCamera: So keep that in mind. The money, the big house, the coat of arms he got later: it was all about winning that position back. But first, he had to go to school. It's five minutes down the road.

routeCard.note: Enter through the Shakespeare Centre on Henley Street. Timed entry.

river.name: The river: the statue, the theatre and the bridge
river.story: Walk here along the river from the church. Bancroft Gardens, by the canal basin. The statue is Shakespeare, with four of his characters around him: Hamlet; Lady Macbeth; Falstaff, a fat, funny knight; and Prince Hal, a young prince who becomes king. Clopton Bridge was built around 1484 by Hugh Clopton, the same man who built New Place. There's a market along Waterside until 6, so it will be busy.
river.onCamera: Shakespeare died 400 years ago. But you've probably quoted him without knowing it. His words are in the way we talk, his plays shaped how England sees its own history, and this whole town still lives off his name. So what did he actually leave behind?
facts: 'Green-eyed monster.' 'A wild-goose chase.' 'It's all Greek to me.' All of these reached everyday English through his plays. People say he invented 1,700 words. That's an exaggeration, but hundreds of words and phrases came to us through him.

He also shaped how England sees its own past. He made King Richard the Third into a famous villain, while writing for Queen Elizabeth the First, whose grandfather had taken Richard's crown. And in 1944, during the Second World War, the British government paid for a film of his play Henry the Fifth, about an English king who invades France and wins. It was made to lift spirits around D-Day.
river.closeOnCamera: And this theatre opened on 23 April 1932, the day Stratford celebrates his birthday. It was designed by Elisabeth Scott. She was 29, and the only woman out of 70 architects in the competition. A glove-maker's son from a small country town. And 400 years later: a theatre, a statue, and the words we speak.

coldOpen.title: Cold open
facts: The hook: 'Everyone knows this man as a poet. But there's another story about him that I'd like to tell you.'
What this is: one afternoon walking through Shakespeare's whole life, in the town where he was born, got rich, and is buried.
The promise: a family that lost everything, a man who won it all back, and a grave with a curse on it.

signOff.title: Closing sign-off
facts: Where you are: by the river, under his statue.
The recap: born into a family in trouble, rich from owning a theatre, buried in a grave he paid for, and still in the words we use.
The ask: like and subscribe, and tell me where I should go next.
